extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, patent practitioners, law students, and general readers interested in patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what patent claims are, how they must be drafted (structure, wording, categories) and how they are interpreted under different legal systems (EPC, US), for the purpose of obtaining and enforcing patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define scope / notice function
rubrics_metrics.description: In a patent or patent application, the claims define in technical terms the extent, i.e. the scope, of the protection conferred by a patent, or the protection sought in a patent application. This is termed as the 'notice function' of a patent claim—to warn others of what they must not do if they are to avoid infringement liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are paramount in prosecution and litigation. See MPEP §2173 ('Claims Must Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim the Invention'). The claims should be precise and clear enough to give the public notice of what is claimed (Nautilus v. Biosig discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of at least one claim in application
rubrics_metrics.description: In most modern patent laws, patent applications must have at least one claim, which are critical defining elements of the patent and the primary subject of examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some laws permit obtaining a date of filing without any claim; however, generally prepare at least one claim for filing because claims are the principal subject of examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC requirement: claims expressed in terms of technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the European Patent Convention (EPC), a claim must define the matter for which the protection is sought in terms of technical features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical features can be structural (e.g., a nail, a rivet) or functional (e.g., fastening means). See EPC Article 84 and EPO Guidelines: claims should be formulated around technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: European two-part form / pre-characterising portion
rubrics_metrics.description: In an independent claim in Europe, the preamble is everything which precedes the expression 'characterized in that' or 'characterized by' in a claim written according to the 'two-part form'; this preamble is regarded as known in the closest prior art and is sometimes called the 'pre-characterizing portion'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-part form to distinguish known combination (preamble) from the novel features (characterizing portion); decisions (e.g., T 0443/11) discuss application of this form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim parts (preamble, transitional phrase, limitations, purpose clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may include: a preamble that recites the class of the invention; a 'transitional' phrase that characterizes the elements that follow; a set of 'limitations' that together describe the invention; and optionally, a purpose clause that further describes the operation or goal of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble may or may not limit claim scope. Limitations should describe interacting/cooperating elements. Purpose clauses (wherein/whereby/thereby) typically limit scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase selection and effect on scope ('comprising' vs 'consisting of' etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases such as 'comprising', 'containing' and 'including' are open (inclusive) and mean 'having at least the following elements'; 'consisting of' and 'consisting essentially of' are more limiting (exclusive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the US, 'consisting of' excludes additional limitations, while 'consisting essentially of' excludes additional limitations that would 'materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention. Choice of transitional phrase materially affects claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations should describe interacting/cooperating elements (combination vs aggregation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of limitations should be described as though they interact or cooperate to achieve the desired result; a combination requires joint operation, while an aggregation is merely adding separate contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft limitations to show mutuality of action (cooperation) when claiming a combination; avoid wording that suggests mere aggregation unless intended (see case law discussing combination vs aggregation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose/wherein/whereby clauses limit scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional purpose clauses (e.g., 'wherein', 'whereby', 'thereby') further describe the overall operation or goal and typically limit the scope of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use purpose clauses when you want to tie a structural or functional limitation to an intended effect; be aware these clauses can be treated as limiting during claim construction (see In re Roemer, Griffin v. Bertina).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims (structure and strategic use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims stand on their own; dependent claims refer to earlier claims, assume all their limitations, and add restrictions. Each dependent claim is, by law, narrower than the claim upon which it depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims clarify/broaden understanding of terms in the independent claim (doctrine of claim differentiation presumption). Use dependent claims as fall-back positions and to claim preferred embodiments. Dependent claims can survive if an independent claim is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims: reference rules and fee/counting consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple dependent claims reference more than one other claim and must reference specific claims and do so in the alternative; rules for these are specific and, in some jurisdictions (e.g., U.S.), multiple dependent claims are counted for filing/fee purposes according to the number of claims they reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft multiple dependent claims carefully (correct alternative phrasing). Be mindful of excess-claim fees at the USPTO; multiple dependent claims are common in Europe but costly in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim categories / statutory categories of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can be categorized by what they claim: product (material/apparatus/system), activity (process/method/use). In the United States, the four statutory categories are processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose claim categories appropriate to the invention and jurisdiction. Some subject matter (printed matter, signals) may not fit statutory categories in the U.S. but may be treated differently at the EPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter boundaries and controversial process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all subject-matter is patentable in all jurisdictions; e.g., printed matter and signals are problematic under U.S. law, and process claims that involve non-physical transformations (data-to-data, business methods) have been controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of jurisdictional differences and evolving case law (e.g., Alice for abstract ideas). Draft claims with patentable subject-matter considerations in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special/formal claim types may be required for certain inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a particular claim form is required by law for certain inventions (e.g., a 'Swiss-type' claim for second medical use) or is chosen to better catch particular infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider special claim formats mandated or advantageous in the target jurisdiction and field (e.g., second medical use phrasing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation / construction principles (objective, context-sensitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction is not concerned with the author's subjective intent but with what a reasonable person to whom the utterance was addressed would have understood the author to mean; meaning depends on words, context, audience, and background knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims in light of the specification, prosecution history, and ordinary meaning. Context and background are crucial; dictionaries/grammars and case law inform interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor may act as lexicographer (definitions in specification control)
rubrics_metrics.description: In U.S. patent practice, inventors may 'act as their own lexicographer' by giving common words or phrases specific meanings in the specification that differ from normal definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you define terms in the specification, those definitions can control claim construction; ensure definitions are clear and consistently used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standards: BRI (exam) vs Phillips (litigation) and USPTO change
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the USPTO used the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification' (BRI) during examination, while U.S. courts used a narrower standard (Phillips). On November 13, 2018 the USPTO switched to the Phillips standard for AIA proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware which construction standard will apply (examination vs litigation vs AIA/PTAB) as it affects claim wording strategy and how broad or narrow claims will be read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness / clarity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim must be precise and clear enough to give the public clear notice of what is claimed; tolerating imprecision that renders a claim 'insolubly ambiguous' would undermine the public-notice function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to satisfy definiteness requirements (see Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc.). Avoid ambiguous terms or provide clear definitions in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiments language and prosecution consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'in one embodiment', 'in a preferred embodiment', or similar are used in the description to introduce particular implementations; these embodiments may or may not each be claimed specifically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: examiners may treat variations presented as separate inventions requiring individual examination. Use embodiment language strategically to disclose alternatives while preserving claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents and scope expansion risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents can be used to expand the effective scope of claims beyond literal wording, but its application has created unpredictability; jurisdictions have constrained it (e.g., Warner-Jenkinson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on doctrine of equivalents is uncertain; draft clear literal claim coverage and consider fallback dependent claims rather than relying solely on equitable doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC vs US differences in dependency across categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the European Patent Convention, when a claim in one category (e.g., process) depends on a claim from a different category (e.g., product), it is not considered a dependent claim but an independent claim; under U.S. law this is still counted as a dependent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of jurisdiction-specific formal rules when drafting cross-category claims and when counting/formatting dependent claims for filing and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting consideration: balance breadth with novelty/non-obviousness risk
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more valuable to obtain claims that include the minimal set of limitations that differentiate an invention over the prior art; however, fewer limitations increase the risk of the claim covering prior art and being rejected for obviousness or lack of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically draft claims to be as broad as possible while including necessary novel limitations; use dependent claims and multiple claim scopes to manage risk.
